https://www.dw.com/en/drought-threatens-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IPa0 Cargo ships anchor near Petrovaradin, Serbia, on the Danube amid extremely low levels of water following an extended period of drought Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure. In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube. Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria , Slovakia , Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania. DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others. Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest , and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country. Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely. Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity. In Prahovo (eastern Serbia), the Danube's low water level has revealed the remains of a German WW II warship Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy. Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week. Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch. Romania's navy carried out a controlled blast of submerged rocks to allow more water to flow into the eastern branch of the Danube Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one. Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production. Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics. Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower. The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade , which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production. In Hungary, dropping water levels of the Danube threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production. Slovakia, Austria less affected In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought. In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages. Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities. Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts. In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources. Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria. The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity. At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity. The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world. These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market. This article was originally published in German. Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment ForMin Toiu discusses with Ukrainian counterpart on energy sector and Russian drones in national airspace The energy sector and Russian drones in national airspace were on the agenda of the telephone conversation between the Romanian and Ukrainian interim Foreign Ministers, Oana Toiu and Andrii Sybiha. ''Neighbors help each other whenever possible, and this was the subject of the phone conversation I had with the Ukrainian Foreign Minister, Andrii Sybiha,'' Toiu wrote on X ob Friday. she said she ''presented the implications of the extremely low level of the Danube on our nuclear energy production and we discussed ways to maintain energy supplies from Ukraine, based on the production capacity of Ukrainian nuclear power plants and the maintenance schedule.'' ''The conversation fits into the line of the very good dialogue between our respective ministries (Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan and Deputy Prime Minister Denys shmyhal). Romania has decided today to declare a state of emergency on the energy market, as a result of the severe drought. These circumstances have necessitated the preventive shutdown of one of the reactors at the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant, and during peak hours we will also rely on energy produced in Ukraine,'' Oana Toiu detailed. The foreign minister mentions that ''within the framework of our strategic partnership, in May, our presidents agreed to build a 400 kV high-voltage power line between our countries, and today's situation represents yet another example of how the interconnection of energy networks brings benefits to Romania, Ukraine, and the European Union's energy market, especially since energy is, without a doubt, a vital element for our economies and directly influences the cost and quality of life of citizens.'' Oana Toiu also says she addressed the situation created by the war in the neighboring country. ''During the conversation, I expressed my solidarity and compassion following another night of barbaric Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, resulting in numerous civilian casualties and entire families killed. I received an update on the security situation, as well as information about Ukraine's needs on the front line and in view of the coming winter. We had an exchange of views on security developments in the Black sea, including regarding the Russian drone incursion into Romania's airspace and the downing of three Russian UAVs by the Romanian Air Force in the past week,'' she added. The acting foreign minister pointed out that ''the sustained attacks on civilian vessels in the Black sea have a profound impact on navigation safety and on the conduct of legitimate economic activities, such as the Maritime Corridor to the ports of Greater Odesa and the CPC terminal, which ensures Romania's supply of crude oil.'' https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday pitched using artificial intelligence to streamline administrative procedures for European businesses as part of a broader push to simplify commerce and boost the EU's competitiveness. Speaking at a behind-closed-doors meeting of the European People's Party in Taormina, Sicily, on Oct. 12, von der Leyen said the Commission would introduce an "only once" approach to business reporting. This would let companies submit information once, with AI helping public administrations use the data. Von der Leyen argued that European companies repeatedly have to report the same information to public authorities, wasting time that businesses — and Europe — cannot afford, according to a copy of her speech seen by POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement "And this is why we will introduce 'Only Once', to report data only once – and with the help of AI the administration will ensure efficient use," she said. The speech marks the first time von der Leyen has explicitly pitched using AI specifically to reduce businesses' administrative workload. The "only once" principle itself is not new. The Commission already included it in its EU Inc. proposal presented in March 2026, which aims to create a harmonized corporate framework allowing companies to establish and operate businesses more easily across the bloc. Under the EU Inc. proposal, companies could submit information once through an EU-level digital interface, with relevant data automatically transmitted between authorities. However, the proposal does not specifically envisage using AI to carry out that process. Von der Leyen did not provide details on how the AI-supported system would operate, whether it would apply to all businesses or when the Commission intends to introduce it. In her speech, the Commission president also encouraged governments to get on board with simplification efforts by signing a pact not to add extra requirements when transposing EU-mandated legislation into national regulations. Advertisement Advertisement The central principle, von der Leyen wrote in a letter to EU leaders sent Oct. 12, is that "a rule agreed at European level cannot become more complex when transposed or implemented nationally." Under the proposed pact, capitals would have to identify and justify additional national requirements that go beyond EU legislation, including assessing their impact on businesses and the single market. Zoya Shefatlovich contributed to reporting
